assign.title: Load the minion skill first. Budget: $2. READ-ONLY scoping; change no files except your own task log. The owner's idea:

log.msg: Eyeballs scope ($2 budget, read-only). Reuse found: Server/Browser.mjs (one shared headless Chromium, never a window, never the owner's own Chrome); site MCP `shot` (fresh headless page -> png, pixels only) and `eval` (DOM truth in a tab, but refuses the owner's own connected tabs -- 'agents never eval or claim a connected tab'); ext/Shots (screenshot+diff system, generic pages, not live-chat-shaped); public/framework/ux/Dictate/test/*.mjs (active-session.mjs, chat-sent.mjs, watch.mjs etc: throwaway scripts that open a headless page via Browser.mjs, page.goto the chat, page.evaluate to read window state -- the closest existing pattern, but one-shot and not a reusable class or MCP tool). No prior 'eyeballs'/screen-watcher session found; no persistent on-demand live-chat-read tool exists yet.

Design (smallest version, law 6 -- extend, don't duplicate): a new class `ChatWatch` in ext/Playwright (new home, since no such ext exists -- Server/Browser.mjs is node-only infra, not a reader). Methods: `look(url)` -> opens (or reuses) one headless context+page via Browser.browser(), page.goto the chat URL, page.evaluate() to pull chat bubbles' innerText in DOM order (same approach as Dictate/test/*.mjs), returns {bubbles:[...], at}; optional `shot()` for a png via the same page. `watch(url, {every})` is NOT a setInterval+fetch poll -- repo law is stream not poll -- so instead of a timer loop inside the tool, a thin node script (`Server/ChatWatch.mjs`, run once as a background task like other Server/*.mjs scripts) calls `look()` every N seconds (N>=5, never sub-second) and appends one JSONL line per snapshot to the session's own folder (e.g. `<session>/chat-watch.jsonl`), which any agent tails live with the existing JSONL `watch()`/`live()` reader -- no new poll loop for the AGENT, it just reads a stream. On-demand use: expose `look()` as a Servex MCP tool so a mastermind can call it directly without starting the background snapshotter.

Risks/cost: a second long-lived headless Chromium context costs ~100-200MB RAM; must go through Browser.browser() (shared instance, reaped by Servex/Lifecycle.js if orphaned/stale) not a fresh chromium.launch(). Must open its OWN context/page on the chat URL -- never page_set/eval against the owner's live connected tab (site MCP explicitly refuses this: 'tab N is the owner's window, not yours'). The chat page's mic must be faked/muted in that context since it is a fresh unauthenticated context, not the owner's session, so it likely has no real mic access anyway -- worth confirming the chat page tolerates that rather than erroring. A hidden/background tab freezes rAF/ResizeObserver-driven layout (doc: hidden tabs do not lay out) -- fine since we only read innerText/DOM, not visual layout, except the optional shot() which needs the page actually rendering (use shot's own fresh-page-per-call pattern for pixels, not a long-hidden one).

First step/test: write `Server/ChatWatch.mjs` with one exported `look(url)` built on Browser.mjs, prove it against a real chat page by page.goto + extract bubble text, reusing the selector Dictate/test/active-session.mjs already uses. Test: run it twice 5s apart against a fixture page, assert the second call sees an appended bubble and no window/process is left running after Browser.close(). Only after that works would an MCP tool wrapper or the JSONL snapshot loop be added -- both are thin wrappers on the same `look()`, so build that one thing first (CLAUDE.md law 1, ASAP).

finish.outcome: Scoped only (read-only, no files changed). PARTLY exists: Server/Browser.mjs + site MCP shot/eval + Dictate/test/*.mjs cover the headless-browser half; nothing reads a live chat into a throttled JSONL stream yet. Smallest build: a ChatWatch.look(url) on Browser.mjs reusing Dictate test's DOM-extraction pattern, a Server/ChatWatch.mjs snapshot loop (>=5s, appends JSONL, never setInterval+fetch polling by the agent), and an MCP wrapper for on-demand use. Full findings logged above.
